newsitem.title: USA: New estimates show spending drop in Medicaid plan.
newsitem.headline: New estimates show spending drop in Medicaid plan.

text.p: The Congressional Budget Office Thursday released new forecasts showing lower-than- expected spending for the federal Medicare and Medicaid health programs during the next five years.
The new projections show overall spending under the Medicare health program for the nation's elderly running $40 billion below previous, April 1996 projections for the five-year period.
Federal spending on Medicaid, which provides health care for the poor, elderly and disabled will be $82 billion less than previously expected over that time frame.
The projections are important because they will form the basis for balanced budget negotiations between the White House and Congress.

The politically popular Medicare program, which provides health insurance to 38 million senior citizens, is expected to be a key point of contention in budget negotiations between the White House and congressional Republicans.

President Clinton is expected to send Congress a budget plan next month calling for about $100 billion in Medicare reductions over five years. The reductions will come mainly from cuts to doctors, hospitals and other health providers.
The White House is not expected to call for any increase in Medicare premiums.

The plan is expected to extend the solvency of Medicare's Part A trust fund, which covers hospital care. The Medicare trustees estimate that Part A will run a deficit beginning in 2001 unless policy changes are made.
A key Republican lawmaker said the Medicare numbers were only marginally better for the Part A trust fund and said major steps were needed to ensure the program's solvency.
Spending for Medicare Part A, which covers hospital care, will be $872.4 billion during the five-year period. That is $15.5 billion lower than previously forecast from 1998-2002.

"This new report is disappointing and unfortunately dashes any hopes that Medicare's financial condition was significantly improving, or that Medicare would go bankrupt later than expected," California Republican Rep. Bill Thomas said in a statement.

Overall federal spending on Medicaid is expected to be $618 billion over the five-year period. States, which share the costs of the program with the federal government, will spend another $449 billion, the CBO said.

The White House will also call for reductions in Medicaid. Congressional sources say the administration will submit a plan setting a per capita cap on spending under the program, which is now an open-ended entitlement.
Annual per person spending would be tied to increases in U.S. gross domestic product.
